title: Thimble and the Shiny Button
markdown:
By the Whispering Peaks, those ancient storytellers, snowy paths murmured secrets to the streams that tumbled down, chattering like excited children. Between the peaks the tinkling of bells, like tiny cheerful birds, would flutter, heralding the grand Sunstone Festival.

This was home to Morwen, a witch whose magic was as quiet and useful as her perfectly darned socks, heart like a warm hearth. Her constant shadow, boundless and sometimes bewildering in devotion, was Thimble.

Thimble was not exactly a cat, though he purred like one and adored a sunbeam nap. A fluffy round bundle, paws as determined as a badger with a buried nut, a will of iron when he felt it needed. His heroic stubbornness was about to cause a small important wobble in festival preparations.

It was not the charm. It was the button. That was the trouble, and also, as it happened, the help.

“Fiddlesticks,” Morwen hummed, fingers on her worn spellbook. “Where has my Moonpetal Charm gone?” Delicate silver filigree holding a single shimmering moonpetal, essential for catching the Sunstone’s first light. Without it the sunbeams would not power the village for the year. A dismal shame, if one were in the mood for dismay.

Whoosh. Thimble bounded from beneath the favourite armchair, smug wiggle in a fluffy tail, and deposited a small slightly grubby but undeniably shiny brass button at her feet.

“A button, Thimble?” A finely arched eyebrow, the look that made him feel a tiny bit guilty. “Very round of you. Quite shiny. Not quite the Moonpetal Charm.”

He chirped, insistent, nudging the button. Morwen’s heart sank a little, a pebble into a well. She loved him more than the stars. His idea of heroism sometimes involved trading precious things for peculiar trinkets.

Then a shadow so big it made you squint fell over the cottage. Zephyr the dragon: shiny scales, wings that could flap up a storm, trying very hard to be mysterious.

“Greetings, mortals,” he rumbled, aiming for gravel and landing near indigestion. “I sense a disturbance. Of great importance.”

“You sense Thimble traded the Moonpetal Charm for a button,” Morwen said dryly. “You were watching from the crags.”

Zephyr’s magnificent head dipped. “A curious transaction. An object of great power, essential to the community, exchanged for a simple disc of gleaming metal.” He puffed his chest. “My presence is coincidental. I was observing atmospheric pressures. And the unusual migration of the cloud-sheep.”

“Right.” Morwen clapped. “The only way to get it back is to find who Thimble traded with. You can carry us to the Whispering Valley. That is where he was, chasing butterflies and engaging in diplomatic trade.”

“The Whispering Valley.” Zephyr drew himself up. “Considerable peril. Mist. Unknown dangers.”

“Grog the ogre shepherd keeps his fluffy sheep there,” Morwen said, hefting her well-worn satchel. “And that is where Thimble went. If you are going to be mysterious, you might at least be punctual.”

In a flash Morwen and Thimble perched on Zephyr’s broad back. Wind a wild song. Below, snow-dusted land like a white quilt stitched with sapphire streams. Pine and distant snow.

They landed near a narrow swaying rope bridge over a deep gorge. Moonlight like spilled milk on frayed ropes. “Aha,” Zephyr declared, extending one mighty claw. “The great chasm. Only the bravest dare cross.”

Thimble scurried across like a furry blur, paws gripping as if glued. Morwen followed, steps sure, the bridge swaying with each gust. Zephyr had trouble with the mysterious part. He paused to strike intimidating poses, wobbled, and looked more awkward than awe-inspiring.

“Are you quite all right?” Morwen called, already halfway.

Zephyr huffed smoke. “Perfectly. Contemplating the structural integrity of this rudimentary contraption. A dragon’s work is never done. One must be vigilant.”

On the other side Grog tended his flock. Immense, nose like a lumpy potato, ears drooping like damp leaves. He watched them with an unnervingly steady gaze.

“Well now,” he rumbled, surprisingly gentle. “Fancy seeing you three. A journey for a little witch and her interesting companion. What’s young Thimble got there?” A thick thumb at the shiny button, still clutched.

Morwen sighed. “Thimble. Did you trade the Moonpetal Charm for this button?”

Thimble, ears drooping, gave a reluctant nod, and nudged the button as if to say: but it is so shiny.

“That button belongs to a very grumpy badger,” Grog said, a twinkle in deep-set eyes. “Complaining this morning about losing his favourite shiny thing. Digging holes all day. Very cross.”

Morwen’s jaw dropped. “You traded the charm for a button belonging to a grumpy badger who had lost his favourite shiny thing?” Thimble was now interested in a particularly fluffy sheep.

He chirped: he seemed sad.

“And you noticed,” Morwen said to Grog, who was stroking a nearby sheep. “You saw the trade.”

“Someone has to. These mountains are full of folk who are not paying attention to the little things. Thimble is a determined sort. I reckon he felt bad for that badger. They’re a bit like us. Sometimes we get grumpy about what we’ve lost, and then we wish we had not been so cross.”

Morwen looked at Thimble, batting the button. At Grog’s quiet understanding. Thimble’s heroism was not boastful. It was noticing when someone was unhappy, even if the method was peculiar.

“Of course. Helping does not always look as you expect. Sometimes it looks like a shiny button.”

It was not the charm. It was the button.

Zephyr stepped forward, clearing a throat like pebbles in a tin. “I admit my mystique was overdone. A trifle theatrical.” Sheepish. “Good to know such thoughtful creatures reside here, even if their methods are unconventional.”

“To get the charm back,” Morwen asked, “what would you trade for the button, so we can return it to the badger?”

Grog scratched his chin. His gaze fell on a small delicate flower in Morwen’s satchel, petals the colour of a sliver of moon. “That moonpetal. Smells lovely. My mountain roses are looking sad. They could use extra beauty.”

She looked at the charm Grog held out, then the button, then the single perfect moonpetal, silvery reminder of the festival. Cool and fragile. She plucked it. “This is worth more than a button. It is worth helping a friend. And knowing that Thimble, in his own way, was trying to help too.”

Grog beamed, a rare sunrise. “Done deal.” He handed her the Moonpetal Charm.

Festival bells chimed in the distance, a symphony of joyful sound. Morwen, Thimble, and Zephyr made their way back. The Sunstone, high on its pedestal, captured the first glorious light of dawn, thanks to the Moonpetal Charm, and the festival was a joyous affair, filled with laughter and dancing. Zephyr, no longer attempting mystery, regaled the crowd with a surprisingly funny tale of his wobbly crossing of the rope bridge, even acting out his precarious poses. Morwen and Thimble sat together on a patch of soft grass, Morwen scratching Thimble behind his fluffy ears, a gesture he adored. The badger, it was later reported, got his button back and was only moderately grumpy, which for a badger counted as a festival. Morwen did not give a speech about understanding. The charm did its work, and Thimble, who had caused the wobble, kept one paw on her sock, which was how you knew a trade could go wrong and still come right. The peaks, if they murmured, kept the details to themselves.
characters: Morwen (witch whose magic is as useful as darned socks), Thimble (a fluffy companion with heroic stubbornness), Zephyr (a dragon who is trying very hard to seem mysterious)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain adventure fantasy for ages 9-10
author: StoryGen Community
